description: Design a neural signal acquisition system from electrode selection through amplifier design to wireless telemetry, sized to the target signal type and recording environment.

steps.description: Define the target neural signal type, its amplitude range, bandwidth, and spatial resolution requirement to anchor every downstream design decision.

inputs.name: clinical-or-research-objective
inputs.desc: What the recording system must measure (e.g., single-unit spikes for BCI cursor control, ECoG for seizure localization, EEG for sleep staging)

inputs.name: implant-constraints
inputs.desc: Whether the system is non-invasive (scalp), minimally invasive (epidural/subdural), or fully implanted (intracortical), plus any size or weight limits

outputs.name: signal-specification
outputs.desc: Target signal type (EEG, ECoG, LFP, single-unit, EMG), amplitude range (microvolts to millivolts), bandwidth (0.1-100 Hz for EEG, 300-6000 Hz for spikes, DC-300 Hz for LFP), and spatial resolution requirement

outputs.name: channel-count-requirement
outputs.desc: Number of recording channels needed from spatial coverage analysis and information throughput requirement

process: Map the clinical or research objective to the neural signal type that carries the information. Single-unit spikes give the highest information per channel but require intracortical penetration. ECoG gives good spatial resolution (1-4 mm electrode spacing) without penetrating cortex. EEG is non-invasive but spatially blurred (centimeter-scale).

Define the amplitude range: EEG is 10-100 uV, ECoG is 50-500 uV, LFP is 0.1-1 mV, single-unit spikes are 50-500 uV at the electrode but can be as low as 20 uV for distant neurons. This range sets the amplifier input-referred noise floor target (must be at least 5x below signal for adequate SNR).

Define the bandwidth: EEG and LFP signals occupy DC to 300 Hz. Spike waveforms require 300-6000 Hz minimum, 300-10000 Hz preferred. Full broadband recording (0.1-10000 Hz) captures both but increases data rate. Sampling rate must be at least 2x the upper bandwidth (Nyquist), practically 3-5x for anti-aliasing filter roll-off.

Estimate channel count from coverage requirements. For BCI cursor control with intracortical arrays, 96-256 channels in motor cortex. For epilepsy monitoring with ECoG grids, 64-256 channels over suspected focus. For research EEG, 32-256 channels for source localization. Each channel multiplied by the data rate gives total throughput.

steps.description: Select or design the electrode array from the signal specification, choosing electrode material, geometry, and array configuration to achieve the required impedance and selectivity.

inputs.name: signal-specification
inputs.desc: Target signal type, amplitude, bandwidth, spatial resolution

inputs.name: channel-count-requirement
inputs.desc: Number of channels needed

inputs.name: implant-constraints
inputs.desc: Invasiveness level, size, weight, lifetime requirement

outputs.name: electrode-design
outputs.desc: Electrode type (microelectrode array, ECoG grid, scalp electrode), material (Pt, IrOx, PEDOT:PSS, Ag/AgCl), geometry (site diameter, pitch, shank dimensions), and array configuration

outputs.name: impedance-specification
outputs.desc: Target electrode impedance at 1 kHz per site and expected impedance range, which drives amplifier input impedance requirements

process: Select electrode type from invasiveness and signal type. Intracortical single-unit recording: silicon microelectrode arrays (Utah array: 10x10, 400 um pitch, 1-1.5 mm shank length; Neuropixels: 384 sites on single shank). ECoG: thin-film platinum or PEDOT:PSS on flexible polymer (polyimide or parylene-C), site diameter 200 um to 2 mm. EEG: sintered Ag/AgCl wet electrodes or dry electrodes (gold pins, conductive polymer).

Select electrode material for target impedance and longevity. Bare platinum: 100-500 kOhm at 1 kHz for 15 um diameter sites. Iridium oxide (AIROF or SIROF): 10-100 kOhm, excellent charge injection capacity for combined recording/stimulation. PEDOT:PSS: 10-50 kOhm with lower noise floor but chronic stability questions beyond 6-12 months. Ag/AgCl for EEG: less than 5 kOhm after gel application.

Size the electrode site diameter from spatial selectivity requirement. For single-unit isolation, sites under 30 um diameter. For multi-unit or LFP, 50-200 um. For ECoG macro-contacts, 1-4 mm. Smaller sites have higher impedance (impedance scales roughly as 1/area), which increases thermal noise (Vrms = sqrt(4kTRB) where R is real part of impedance at signal bandwidth B). Calculate thermal noise floor and verify it is below target signal amplitude.

Define array configuration: electrode count, pitch, total footprint, connector. For chronic implants, the connector and cable are often the failure point. Consider integrated wireless to eliminate percutaneous connectors. For acute research, Omnetics or ZIF connectors are standard. Map the array footprint to the target brain region anatomy.

steps.description: Design or select the analog front-end amplifier chain from the electrode impedance and signal specification, targeting the required noise floor, CMRR, and power per channel.

inputs.name: signal-specification
inputs.desc: Signal amplitude range and bandwidth

inputs.name: impedance-specification
inputs.desc: Electrode impedance at 1 kHz and expected range

inputs.name: channel-count-requirement
inputs.desc: Number of channels to amplify

outputs.name: amplifier-specification
outputs.desc: Input-referred noise floor, gain, bandwidth, CMRR, input impedance, power per channel, and ADC resolution

outputs.name: analog-front-end-architecture
outputs.desc: Amplifier topology (AC-coupled capacitive feedback, chopper-stabilized, or direct-coupled), multiplexing strategy, and ADC configuration

process: Set the input-referred noise target. For single-unit recording, the noise floor must be below 5 uVrms to detect 50 uV spikes with SNR of 10 (20 dB). For ECoG, below 2 uVrms. For EEG, below 1 uVrms. The amplifier noise and electrode thermal noise add in quadrature: total noise = sqrt(amp_noise^2 + electrode_thermal_noise^2). If electrode thermal noise dominates, reducing amplifier noise further yields diminishing returns.

Select amplifier topology. Capacitive feedback amplifiers (Intan RHD2164 architecture) are standard for implantable neural recording: AC-coupled with high-pass corner set by capacitor ratio (typically 0.1-1 Hz), mid-band gain of 100-200, input impedance greater than 10 MOhm at 1 kHz. Chopper-stabilized amplifiers reduce flicker noise below 1 Hz but require careful design to avoid chopper artifacts mixing into the neural band. Direct DC-coupled designs are needed for spreading depolarization research.

Size the ADC: resolution must capture the full dynamic range. Neural signals span about 60 dB (1 mV artifacts to 10 uV spikes). A 16-bit ADC with 1 mV input range gives 15 nV LSB, adequate. In practice, 10-12 bits after the programmable gain amplifier is sufficient for most applications. Sampling rate: 30 kSps per channel for spike recording, 1 kSps for LFP/EEG. Total data rate = channels x bits x sample_rate.

Calculate power budget per channel. State-of-art neural amplifiers achieve 1-5 uW per channel. For a 1024-channel system, the analog front-end alone draws 1-5 mW. Add digitization power (ADC, multiplexing). For implantable systems, total power must stay within the heat dissipation limit: less than 40 mW/cm2 on brain surface to avoid thermal tissue damage (1 degree C rise threshold). CMRR must exceed 80 dB to reject 50/60 Hz interference and motion artifacts.

steps.description: Design the data path from digitized neural signals to the external processing system, including on-implant data reduction, wireless link, and power delivery.

inputs.name: analog-front-end-architecture
inputs.desc: Channel count, sample rate, bit depth, total raw data rate

inputs.name: amplifier-specification
inputs.desc: Power budget and heat constraint

outputs.name: telemetry-design
outputs.desc: Wireless protocol, data rate, on-implant compression strategy, transmit power, and antenna design

outputs.name: power-delivery-design
outputs.desc: Power source (battery, inductive, ultrasonic), charging protocol, and total power budget

process: Calculate raw data rate: 1024 channels x 30 kSps x 16 bits = 491 Mbps raw. This exceeds any practical implantable wireless link. Data reduction is mandatory. Option 1: transmit only spike times and waveform snippets (detect on-chip, transmit 1-ms waveforms at each threshold crossing, reducing bandwidth by 10-100x). Option 2: transmit LFP only (downsample to 1 kSps, 16 Mbps). Option 3: on-chip spike sorting reduces to firing rates (below 1 Mbps for 1024 channels at 100 Hz update).

Select wireless link. Near-field inductive (13.56 MHz): reliable, short range (1-3 cm), data rate to 10 Mbps, can share coil with power delivery. UWB (3.1-10.6 GHz): higher data rate (up to 100 Mbps), better range (10 cm through tissue), but higher power and more complex antenna. Bluetooth LE: 2 Mbps, good ecosystem but limited for high-channel-count full-bandwidth. Calculate link margin: path loss through 1 cm tissue at carrier frequency, antenna gain (on-implant antenna is small, typically -10 to -20 dBi), receiver sensitivity.

Design power delivery. For implantable systems, transcutaneous inductive power is standard: an external coil driven at 100 kHz to 13.56 MHz couples to an implanted coil. Coupling coefficient k depends on coil alignment and separation (typically k = 0.05-0.2 for 1-2 cm separation). Power transfer efficiency = k^2 x Q1 x Q2 / (1 + k^2 x Q1 x Q2). Size the coils from power requirement (typically 10-50 mW for a 1024-channel system after data reduction). Regulate received power with LDO or switched-mode regulator. For battery-backed systems, lithium primary cells give 5-10 years for low-power EEG devices.

Verify SAR compliance: the transmitted RF power must keep specific absorption rate below 1.6 W/kg averaged over 1 g of tissue (FCC) or 2 W/kg over 10 g (ICNIRP). Run thermal simulation: total implant heat dissipation (electronics + coil losses) must not raise adjacent tissue temperature by more than 1 degree C in steady state.

steps.description: Integrate and validate the complete acquisition system from electrode to data output using bench testing, saline testing, and in-vivo verification.

inputs.name: electrode-design
inputs.desc: Electrode array specification

inputs.name: amplifier-specification
inputs.desc: Analog front-end parameters

inputs.name: telemetry-design
inputs.desc: Wireless link configuration

inputs.name: power-delivery-design
inputs.desc: Power system configuration

outputs.name: system-validation-report
outputs.desc: Measured noise floor, CMRR, crosstalk, data integrity, power consumption, thermal performance, and recording quality from bench and saline tank testing

outputs.name: acquisition-system-specification
outputs.desc: Finalized system specification with measured performance against requirements

process: Bench test the analog front-end: measure input-referred noise by shorting inputs and recording (calculate RMS in the signal band). Verify CMRR by applying a common-mode sinusoid at 60 Hz and measuring rejection. Measure crosstalk between adjacent channels by driving one channel and measuring coupling to neighbors. Target: crosstalk below -60 dB.

Saline tank test: submerge the electrode array in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, 0.9% NaCl) at 37 degrees C. Measure electrode impedance at 1 kHz using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. Apply known signals through a reference electrode and verify recording fidelity (amplitude accuracy, bandwidth, phase response). Verify that impedance is within specification and uniform across the array (coefficient of variation below 30%).

Wireless link test: measure bit error rate at the operating data rate across the intended separation distance. Verify power delivery efficiency and thermal profile (IR camera or embedded temperature sensor). Run the system at full power for 24 hours and verify thermal steady state does not exceed tissue safety limit.

In-vivo verification (for animal research or first-in-human): record neural signals and verify the presence of expected signal features (spike waveforms with correct width 0.5-2 ms, LFP oscillations at expected frequencies). Calculate SNR of detected spikes. Compare noise floor in-vivo to bench measurements (in-vivo is typically 2-5x higher due to biological noise and motion artifacts). Document any anomalies for design iteration.

description: Build a neural signal processing pipeline from raw digitized signals through artifact removal, spike detection, spike sorting, and neural decoding.

steps.description: Remove artifacts from raw neural recordings using methods matched to each artifact source: line noise, motion, stimulation, and biological interference.

inputs.name: raw-neural-data
inputs.desc: Digitized multi-channel neural recording with metadata (sample rate, channel map, recording conditions)

inputs.name: recording-metadata
inputs.desc: Electrode type, reference scheme, known artifact sources (stimulation timing, movement markers)

outputs.name: cleaned-neural-data
outputs.desc: Neural recording with artifacts removed or attenuated, preserving signal features

outputs.name: artifact-removal-report
outputs.desc: Which methods were applied, how much variance was removed, and any channels flagged as unrecoverable

process: Apply a notch filter at 50/60 Hz (and harmonics) to remove power line interference only if line noise exceeds 5 uV peak. Use a zero-phase IIR notch (Q factor 30-50) or subtract a sinusoidal template estimated from the data. Avoid aggressive notch filters near neural frequencies of interest.

Remove motion and muscle artifacts using Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Run ICA on the multi-channel data (FastICA or Infomax). Identify artifact components by their spatial topography (frontal bilateral for eye blinks, lateral for saccades, high-frequency broadband for EMG) and temporal characteristics (correlation with EOG/EMG reference channels if available). Remove identified components and reconstruct. For intracortical recordings, common average referencing (CAR) removes shared motion artifacts: subtract the mean across all channels from each channel.

Handle stimulation artifacts (if recording during stimulation): blank the stimulation window (typically 0.5-2 ms after each pulse) and interpolate, or use template subtraction by averaging the artifact waveform across hundreds of stimulation events and subtracting the template from each occurrence. For exponential decay artifacts from charge redistribution, fit and subtract an exponential model.

Flag and exclude bad channels: channels with impedance greater than 2 MOhm (for microelectrodes) or sustained 60 Hz amplitude greater than 50 uV after filtering, or channels with flat signals (broken connections). Interpolate from neighbors for surface arrays (EEG, ECoG) using spherical spline interpolation. For penetrating arrays, simply exclude dead channels from downstream analysis.

steps.description: Detect action potential waveforms from cleaned extracellular recordings and sort them into putative single neuron clusters using feature extraction and clustering.

inputs.name: cleaned-neural-data
inputs.desc: Artifact-cleaned high-pass filtered neural recording (300-6000 Hz bandpass)

outputs.name: sorted-spike-trains
outputs.desc: For each identified neuron: timestamps of spikes, mean waveform, cluster quality metrics (isolation distance, L-ratio, ISI violation rate)

outputs.name: spike-sorting-quality-report
outputs.desc: Number of single units, multi-units, and noise clusters per channel, with quality metrics

process: Bandpass filter the cleaned data to 300-6000 Hz (4th-order Butterworth, zero-phase). Detect spikes by threshold crossing: set threshold at -4 to -5 times the median absolute deviation (MAD) of the filtered signal divided by 0.6745 (robust noise estimate from Quiroga et al.). Extract 1.5-ms waveform snippets centered on each threshold crossing (typically 48 samples at 30 kSps: 16 pre, 32 post).

Extract features for clustering. Principal Component Analysis (PCA): compute the first 3-6 PCs of the waveform matrix. These capture waveform shape differences between neurons (peak height, trough width, asymmetry). Alternative: wavelet decomposition coefficients selected by Lilliefors test for non-normality (features that best separate clusters).

Cluster the feature space into putative single units. Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM): fit K Gaussians using expectation-maximization, select K by BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion). Alternative: density-based clustering (DBSCAN) for non-Gaussian clusters. For high-channel-count probes (Neuropixels), use template matching approaches (Kilosort): project data onto a template bank, assign spikes to templates, merge/split templates iteratively.

Validate sorting quality. For each cluster: (1) ISI violation rate: fewer than 1% of inter-spike intervals below 1.5 ms refractory period indicates a well-isolated single unit. (2) Isolation distance: Mahalanobis distance between cluster and nearest neighbor, greater than 20 is good. (3) L-ratio: below 0.1 indicates low contamination. (4) Waveform stability across the recording session (drift detection by plotting amplitude over time). Classify units as single-unit (passes all), multi-unit (fails ISI), or noise (fails waveform consistency).

steps.description: Extract and analyze local field potential features including power spectra, event-related potentials, and time-frequency decompositions for neural state characterization.

inputs.name: cleaned-neural-data
inputs.desc: Artifact-cleaned broadband neural recording

outputs.name: lfp-features
outputs.desc: Power spectral densities by frequency band (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma, high-gamma), event-related potentials, and time-frequency spectrograms

outputs.name: neural-state-markers
outputs.desc: Identified neural states (e.g., sleep stages from delta/spindle power, attention from alpha desynchronization, motor preparation from beta suppression)

process: Low-pass filter and downsample to 1 kSps (anti-alias filter at 400 Hz before decimation). Re-reference if needed: bipolar montage for localized signals, Laplacian for spatial filtering of ECoG/EEG. For LFP from penetrating arrays, local re-referencing between nearby contacts improves spatial specificity.

Compute power spectral density using Welch's method (2-second Hanning windows, 50% overlap) or multitaper method (3-5 tapers for optimal bias-variance trade-off at each frequency). Extract band power by integrating PSD: delta (0.5-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), low gamma (30-70 Hz), high gamma (70-200 Hz). High gamma from ECoG is a reliable proxy for local cortical activation.

For event-locked analysis: epoch data around events (stimulus onset, movement onset), average across trials to obtain event-related potentials (ERPs). Compute time-frequency decomposition using Morlet wavelet convolution (wave number 5-7 for good time-frequency trade-off) or short-time Fourier transform. Normalize to baseline period using decibel or z-score transform. Identify event-related spectral perturbations (ERSP): desynchronization (power decrease) or synchronization (power increase) in specific bands.

Derive neural state markers: beta (13-30 Hz) desynchronization over motor cortex indicates motor preparation (onset 500-1000 ms before movement). Alpha (8-13 Hz) suppression over visual cortex indicates visual attention. Theta (4-8 Hz) power in hippocampal recordings marks memory encoding. Sleep staging: high delta + sleep spindles (12-15 Hz) = N2 sleep. Document which markers are present and their reliability (effect size across trials).

steps.description: Decode behavioral variables or intended actions from neural population activity using statistical and machine learning methods matched to the application latency and accuracy requirements.

inputs.name: sorted-spike-trains
inputs.desc: Spike trains from sorted single units

inputs.name: lfp-features
inputs.desc: LFP band power and spectral features

inputs.name: clinical-or-research-objective
inputs.desc: What must be decoded (cursor velocity, grasp type, speech, seizure onset)

outputs.name: decoder-model
outputs.desc: Trained decoder with architecture, parameters, feature set, and performance metrics (correlation, bit rate, latency)

outputs.name: decoding-performance-report
outputs.desc: Offline cross-validated accuracy, information transfer rate in bits per second, and comparison to chance level

process: Select features based on signal type and decoding target. For continuous kinematics (cursor velocity, arm trajectory): firing rates in 50-100 ms bins from motor cortex single units, or high-gamma power from ECoG over motor areas. For discrete classification (grasp type, speech phoneme): firing rate vectors at go-cue aligned epochs, or ECoG time-frequency features in a 500 ms window.

Select decoder architecture by application. For continuous BCI cursor control: Kalman filter (linear, interpretable, low latency) modeling the relationship between neural firing rates and cursor velocity. The ReFIT Kalman filter adds intention estimation during closed-loop control (clamp the inferred target, refit on corrected training data). For discrete classification: linear discriminant analysis (LDA) for low-dimensional, support vector machine for moderate, or recurrent neural network (GRU/LSTM) for temporal patterns in high-dimensional signals.

Train and validate. Split data into training (70%) and test (30%) sets, or use 5-fold cross-validation. For Kalman filter: fit state-transition and observation matrices from training data using least-squares. For classifiers: fit on training features, tune hyperparameters on validation fold. Measure offline performance: Pearson correlation (r) between decoded and actual kinematics for continuous, classification accuracy and confusion matrix for discrete. Calculate information transfer rate: ITR = log2(N) + P*log2(P) + (1-P)*log2((1-P)/(N-1)) bits per trial, where N = number of classes, P = accuracy.

Assess practical performance. Latency budget: time from neural activity to decoded output must be under 100 ms for BCI cursor control (50 ms neural processing delay + 50 ms decode + display). For speech BCI, under 200 ms is acceptable. Measure online performance if possible (closed-loop Fitts's law task: throughput in bits/s, path efficiency). Document session-to-session stability: does decoder performance degrade, and how much recalibration is needed (full retrain, bias correction, or transfer learning with a few trials).

description: Design a biocompatible neural implant from material selection through encapsulation, sterilization, and chronic performance validation following ISO 10993 and regulatory requirements.

steps.description: Select implant materials from the ISO 10993 framework based on contact type, duration, and body tissue, then define the required testing pathway.

inputs.name: implant-functional-requirements
inputs.desc: What the implant must do (record, stimulate, drug delivery), where it is placed (brain, peripheral nerve, spinal cord), and how long it stays (acute under 24h, limited 1-30 days, prolonged over 30 days)

inputs.name: implant-form-factor
inputs.desc: Physical size, shape, and mechanical constraints from the surgical approach and target anatomy

outputs.name: material-selections
outputs.desc: Selected materials for each implant component (substrate, encapsulation, electrode, conductor, connector) with rationale

outputs.name: biocompatibility-test-matrix
outputs.desc: Required ISO 10993 tests mapped to each material and contact category (cytotoxicity, sensitization, irritation, acute systemic toxicity, subchronic toxicity, genotoxicity, implantation, hemocompatibility as applicable)

process: Classify the implant by ISO 10993-1: contact type (surface, external communicating, or implant device), contact tissue (bone, tissue/tissue fluid, blood), and contact duration (limited, prolonged, permanent). A chronic intracortical neural implant is: implant device, tissue/tissue fluid contact, permanent duration. This is the highest risk category requiring the most extensive testing.

Select substrate material. Silicon: well-characterized, standard for Utah and Neuropixels arrays, but brittle and stiff (170 GPa vs brain tissue 1 kPa, 5 orders of magnitude mismatch drives chronic inflammation). Flexible polymers: polyimide (3 GPa, better but still stiff), parylene-C (4 GPa, pinhole-free thin-film conformal coating, USP Class VI), SU-8 (photopatternable but limited biocompatibility data for chronic). For brain implants, compliance matching favors polymer substrates.

Select encapsulation. Hermetic titanium: gold standard for active implantable devices (pacemakers, cochlear implants), zero moisture ingress, but adds bulk. Ceramic (alumina): RF transparent for wireless, hermetic, but brittle. Thin-film encapsulation (parylene-C, 5-20 um): lightweight, conformal, but moisture penetration limits lifetime to 1-5 years depending on thickness and defects. Liquid crystal polymer (LCP): emerging alternative with low moisture absorption.

Map required biocompatibility tests from ISO 10993-1 Table A.1. For a permanent implant in tissue contact: cytotoxicity (ISO 10993-5, cell culture), sensitization (ISO 10993-10, guinea pig or local lymph node), irritation/intracutaneous reactivity, acute systemic toxicity, subchronic toxicity (90-day implant study), genotoxicity (Ames, chromosomal aberration, mouse lymphoma), implantation study (ISO 10993-6, histological evaluation at the implant site), chronic toxicity, and carcinogenicity. Materials with extensive prior use (titanium, medical-grade silicone, parylene-C) may qualify for reduced testing via biological safety justification.

steps.description: Design the implant encapsulation system for moisture protection, mechanical protection, and chronic biocompatibility, verified by accelerated aging.

inputs.name: material-selections
inputs.desc: Materials for each component

inputs.name: implant-form-factor
inputs.desc: Size, shape, mechanical constraints

outputs.name: encapsulation-design
outputs.desc: Encapsulation material, thickness, deposition method, feedthrough design, and expected lifetime

outputs.name: accelerated-aging-protocol
outputs.desc: Test protocol to verify encapsulation integrity: temperature, duration, pass/fail criteria based on impedance, leakage current, and visual inspection

process: Define the moisture barrier requirement from the electronics sensitivity. CMOS circuitry fails when moisture reaches the die: target moisture ingress rate below 10^-3 g/m2/day for multi-year implant life. Hermetic enclosures (titanium, ceramic) achieve effectively zero ingress. Thin-film polymer coatings have finite permeability: parylene-C at 10 um thickness allows ~0.08 g/m2/day at 37 degrees C, giving estimated failure in 1-3 years for bare CMOS, longer if additional moisture getters or conformal coatings are used.

Design feedthroughs for electrical connections passing through the hermetic boundary. For titanium enclosures: glass-to-metal seals or ceramic-to-metal brazed feedthroughs (used in cochlear implants, up to 22 pins). For higher pin counts needed for neural interfaces (100+), thin-film multi-layer feedthroughs on ceramic substrates (alumina with platinum vias) allow higher density. Each feedthrough must maintain hermeticity (leak rate below 10^-8 atm-cc/s He).

Design for chronic mechanical stability. The implant must withstand micromotion between the brain and skull (10-50 um displacement with each heartbeat and respiration). Strain relief at the electrode-cable junction is critical. Flexible interconnects (thin-film metal on polymer) absorb motion. Anchoring: skull screws for the housing, but no rigid attachment between the housing and the intracortical array (allow floating). Calculate mechanical fatigue life from cyclic strain amplitude and material S-N curve.

Define accelerated aging protocol per ASTM F1980: use 60 or 85 degrees C saline soak with an acceleration factor calculated from the Arrhenius equation (Q10 = 2 assumption: each 10 degree C increase doubles aging rate). At 60 degrees C, 1 month equals approximately 4 months at 37 degrees C. At 85 degrees C, 1 month equals approximately 23 months. Monitor electrode impedance weekly, leakage current through encapsulation, and visual inspection under microscope for delamination, cracking, or corrosion. Pass criteria: impedance drift below 50%, no leakage current increase, no visible failure through the target equivalent lifetime.

steps.description: Select and validate a sterilization method compatible with the implant materials and electronics, meeting sterility assurance level requirements.

inputs.name: material-selections
inputs.desc: All implant materials

inputs.name: encapsulation-design
inputs.desc: Encapsulation system and sealed electronics

outputs.name: sterilization-protocol
outputs.desc: Selected method, parameters (temperature, time, gas concentration or radiation dose), and validated sterility assurance level (SAL)

outputs.name: material-compatibility-verification
outputs.desc: Evidence that sterilization does not degrade implant materials or performance beyond acceptable limits

process: Evaluate sterilization methods against material compatibility. Ethylene oxide (EtO): low temperature (37-55 degrees C), compatible with polymers and electronics, but requires aeration to remove toxic residuals (EtO and ethylene chlorohydrin). Standard for polymer-based neural implants. Gamma radiation (25-40 kGy): fast, no residuals, penetrates packaging, but degrades some polymers (PTFE, acetal) and can affect CMOS electronics (total ionizing dose). Electron beam: similar to gamma but less penetration, suitable for surface devices. Steam (autoclave 121 degrees C): incompatible with most polymers and electronics. Vaporized hydrogen peroxide: low temperature, compatible with metals, limited polymer data.

For most neural implants with polymer components and electronics, EtO is the primary choice. Define cycle parameters: 450-600 mg/L EtO concentration, 55 degrees C, 60% relative humidity, 2-4 hour exposure, followed by aeration at 50 degrees C for 8-12 hours minimum. Aeration time is critical: residual EtO on implant surfaces must be below ISO 10993-7 limits (25 mg for contact devices, lower for implants by body weight calculation).

Validate sterility assurance level (SAL) of 10^-6 per ISO 11135 (EtO) or ISO 11137 (radiation). For EtO: perform a half-cycle qualification (expose product at half the normal cycle time, demonstrate adequate bioburden kill, then full cycle provides overkill margin). Determine product bioburden per ISO 11737-1 (average and maximum). Demonstrate at least 6-log reduction from maximum bioburden at half-cycle.

Verify material compatibility post-sterilization: run functional tests on sterilized samples (electrode impedance, amplifier performance, wireless link function, mechanical integrity) and compare to pre-sterilization baseline. For polymer encapsulation, measure molecular weight (GPC) and tensile properties to detect degradation. Any property change beyond specification limits requires a different sterilization method or redesigned materials.

steps.description: Design and execute chronic in-vivo studies to characterize long-term implant performance including signal quality degradation, tissue response, and failure modes.

inputs.name: encapsulation-design
inputs.desc: Encapsulation system with expected lifetime

inputs.name: sterilization-protocol
inputs.desc: Validated sterilization method

inputs.name: electrode-design
inputs.desc: Electrode array specification

outputs.name: chronic-performance-data
outputs.desc: Signal quality (SNR, unit yield) over time, impedance tracking, tissue histology at explant, failure mode analysis

outputs.name: implant-lifetime-assessment
outputs.desc: Estimated functional lifetime with confidence interval, identified failure modes and their timelines, design improvements for next iteration

process: Design the chronic study. For intracortical arrays, a minimum 6-month implant duration demonstrates chronic stability (12 months preferred for regulatory submissions). Species selection: non-human primate for closest brain analogy, rodent for larger cohorts at lower cost. Sample size: minimum 6 animals per group for statistical power on histological endpoints. Define recording schedule: daily for first week, weekly for first month, monthly thereafter. Track electrode impedance at 1 kHz, signal amplitude (peak-to-peak of detected spikes), noise floor (RMS of signal with no detected spikes), unit yield (channels with detectable single units / total channels).

Characterize the foreign body response timeline. Week 1: acute inflammation (activated microglia, edema, albumin leakage from blood-brain barrier disruption). Week 2-4: chronic inflammation onset (reactive astrocytes begin forming glial sheath, macrophage recruitment). Month 1-3: glial scar matures (dense astrocyte sheath 50-200 um thick around implant, neuronal die-back within 50-100 um of electrode surface). Month 3+: stable chronic state. Quantify by immunohistochemistry at explant: GFAP (astrocytes), Iba-1 (microglia), NeuN (neurons) at 50, 100, 200, 500 um from electrode track.

Track signal quality degradation. Typical trajectory for rigid silicon arrays: 50-80% of channels record single units at week 1, declining to 20-40% by month 6 due to glial encapsulation increasing electrode-to-neuron distance. Impedance typically increases 2-5x over 6 months as tissue encapsulates. Flexible arrays show slower degradation (hypothesis: reduced micromotion-driven inflammation). Plot unit yield and mean SNR vs time with 95% confidence intervals.

Identify and classify failure modes. Electrical: broken traces (from chronic flexion), connector failure, encapsulation breach (moisture ingress causing corrosion or short circuits). Biological: glial encapsulation (gradual signal loss), infection (acute, usually from surgical contamination), foreign body reaction to specific materials. Mechanical: implant migration, cable breakage at strain point. For each failure mode, record time-to-failure and build a reliability model (Weibull distribution). Use this data to define the implant's usable lifetime and prioritize design improvements.

description: Design a neurostimulation system from parameter selection through charge safety analysis, current steering, artifact management, and closed-loop adaptation.

steps.description: Define stimulation parameters from the therapeutic target, ensuring charge-balanced waveforms within the electrochemical safety window of the electrode material.

inputs.name: therapeutic-objective
inputs.desc: What the stimulation must achieve (tremor suppression in Parkinson's, seizure termination, pain relief, motor cortex activation for BCI)

inputs.name: electrode-design
inputs.desc: Electrode material, geometry, impedance, and number of contacts available for stimulation

outputs.name: stimulation-parameters
outputs.desc: Waveform shape (biphasic, symmetric/asymmetric), pulse width, frequency, amplitude (current or voltage), inter-phase gap, and duty cycle

outputs.name: charge-safety-analysis
outputs.desc: Charge per phase, charge density, position relative to Shannon safety limit, and maximum safe parameters for the electrode

process: Select waveform shape. Charge-balanced biphasic pulses are mandatory for chronic stimulation to prevent electrode corrosion and tissue damage from net DC charge. Cathodic-first (negative first) is standard for neural activation (depolarizes at the electrode, lower threshold than anodic). Asymmetric biphasic (short cathodic, longer lower-amplitude anodic) is more charge-efficient: the cathodic phase activates, the anodic phase recovers charge at lower amplitude to avoid anodic block. Include an inter-phase gap of 25-100 us between phases to prevent the anodic phase from immediately canceling cathodic activation.

Set pulse width and frequency from the therapeutic literature. Deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's tremor: 60-90 us pulse width, 130-185 Hz frequency, 1-5 mA amplitude (for microelectrodes) or 1-5 V (for macroelectrodes). Cortical stimulation for motor activation: 200-400 us, 50-300 Hz. Spinal cord stimulation for pain: 200-500 us, 40-100 Hz. Vagus nerve stimulation: 250-500 us, 20-30 Hz. Start at the lowest effective parameters and increase to minimize energy consumption and tissue exposure.

Calculate charge per phase: Q = I x PW (for current-controlled) where I is amplitude and PW is pulse width. Charge density = Q / electrode_area. Apply the Shannon safety limit: log(Q/phase) + log(charge_density) should be less than k, where k = 1.5-2.0 (conservative to aggressive). For a 1 mm diameter electrode (area = 0.785 mm2) at 3 mA x 100 us = 0.3 uC/phase: charge density = 0.38 uC/cm2. Log(0.3e-6) + log(0.38) = -6.52 + (-0.42) = -6.94, well within the k=1.5 limit. For microelectrodes (15 um diameter), the small area makes charge density the binding constraint.

Calculate compliance voltage: V_compliance must exceed I_stim x Z_electrode + V_tissue. For a 10 kOhm electrode at 1 mA, 10 V across the electrode plus 1-2 V tissue voltage requires at least 12 V compliance. Higher compliance voltage increases power consumption. For battery-powered implants (3.7 V lithium cell), a charge pump or boost converter is needed to reach typical 12-18 V compliance. This is a major power consumer in implantable stimulators.

steps.description: Design multi-contact current steering strategies to shape the stimulation field for spatial selectivity, using simultaneous multi-electrode activation.

inputs.name: stimulation-parameters
inputs.desc: Waveform and amplitude specifications

inputs.name: electrode-design
inputs.desc: Multi-contact electrode geometry and impedance per contact

outputs.name: current-steering-configuration
outputs.desc: Current allocation across contacts (percentage per contact, polarity), steering resolution, and estimated volume of tissue activated

outputs.name: field-model
outputs.desc: Finite element model of the electric field distribution in tissue, showing isopotential contours and activation volume for each steering configuration

process: Map the target neural structure and the structures to avoid. For DBS in the subthalamic nucleus: target the dorsolateral motor territory (approximately 3x4 mm), avoid the ventral limbic territory (mood side effects) and the medial internal capsule (muscle contractions). The electrode is a cylindrical lead with 4-8 contacts spaced 0.5-1.5 mm apart (Medtronic 3389, Boston Scientific Vercise).

Implement current steering using multiple independent current sources (one per contact). Divide current across contacts to steer the activation volume. For directional leads (Boston Scientific, Abbott) with segmented contacts (3 segments per row, 120 degrees each), allocate current to one segment to steer the field laterally by approximately 1 mm. For ring contacts, vertical steering between adjacent rings shifts the field up/down along the lead axis in 0.5 mm steps.

Build a finite element model of the electrode in tissue. Tissue conductivity: gray matter 0.2 S/m, white matter 0.1 S/m (anisotropic along fiber direction), CSF 1.8 S/m, electrode-tissue interface impedance from electrode material. Apply stimulation current boundary conditions. Solve for the potential field. Estimate the volume of tissue activated (VTA) using an activation threshold of 0.2 V/mm for 90 us pulses (or couple to axon models for precise prediction using the activating function: second spatial derivative of the potential along the axon).

Optimize current allocation to maximize target coverage while minimizing side-effect region activation. This is a constrained optimization: maximize VTA overlap with target region, subject to total current within safety limits and each contact within its charge density limit. In practice, clinicians step through discrete configurations during programming sessions, adjusting by 10-20% current shifts between contacts and evaluating symptom response and side effects.

steps.description: Design the artifact blanking and recovery strategy for systems that must simultaneously record neural signals during active stimulation.

inputs.name: stimulation-parameters
inputs.desc: Waveform timing and amplitude

inputs.name: amplifier-specification
inputs.desc: Recording amplifier bandwidth, recovery time, and dynamic range

outputs.name: artifact-management-design
outputs.desc: Blanking timing, recovery strategy (sample-and-hold, fast recovery amplifier, template subtraction), and residual artifact specification

outputs.name: recording-during-stimulation-protocol
outputs.desc: Achievable recording quality during active stimulation with specified parameters

process: Characterize the stimulation artifact. During a stimulation pulse (100 us at 3 mA through a 10 kOhm electrode), the voltage at the electrode reaches 30 V peak, saturating any neural recording amplifier (full-scale typically 1-5 mV). The artifact has three phases: (1) the stimulation pulse itself (100 us), (2) electrode polarization recovery (exponential decay, 0.5-5 ms time constant depending on electrode material and charge), (3) amplifier recovery from saturation (0.1-10 ms depending on AC coupling time constant).

Design hardware blanking: disconnect the recording input during the stimulation pulse plus a short margin (total blank window: stimulation pulse width + 100-500 us for electrode discharge). During blanking, hold the amplifier output at its pre-blank value (sample-and-hold) to prevent a transient when reconnecting. For 130 Hz stimulation with 500 us total blank window, 6.5% of data is blanked, acceptable for LFP recording (most information is below 100 Hz) but can miss some spikes.

Design post-artifact recovery. Minimize AC coupling time constants: use DC-coupled or very short time constant (10 ms) amplifiers to reduce exponential recovery artifacts. Add a fast-recover circuit that resets the AC coupling capacitor after each blank window. For remaining artifacts, use template subtraction: average the artifact waveform over 50-100 stimulation cycles (triggered on the stimulation sync signal) and subtract the template from each individual artifact.

Validate recording quality during stimulation. Record known neural signals (spike-generating cortex during movement) with and without stimulation. Compare SNR, spike detection rate, and LFP power spectra. The residual artifact after blanking and template subtraction should be below the neural noise floor (less than 5 uV RMS in the spike band, less than 10 uV in the LFP band). If not met, increase blank window or add more averaging to template subtraction.

steps.description: Design a closed-loop neurostimulation system that adjusts stimulation parameters in real time based on detected neural biomarkers.

inputs.name: therapeutic-objective
inputs.desc: What the closed loop must control (tremor, seizure, mood, motor output)

inputs.name: stimulation-parameters
inputs.desc: Stimulation parameter ranges

inputs.name: neural-state-markers
inputs.desc: Available biomarkers from neural recording

outputs.name: closed-loop-controller-design
outputs.desc: Biomarker detection algorithm, control law (on/off, proportional, model-predictive), parameter adjustment range, safety limits, and latency specification

outputs.name: stability-safety-analysis
outputs.desc: Analysis of closed-loop stability (no oscillation, no runaway stimulation), safety bounds, and fallback behavior

process: Select the biomarker for closed-loop control. For Parkinson's disease: beta band (13-30 Hz) power in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) correlates with bradykinesia and rigidity. Elevated beta = more symptoms = need stimulation. As stimulation takes effect, beta power decreases. This creates a natural negative feedback loop. For epilepsy: detect seizure onset signatures (sustained high-frequency oscillations 80-500 Hz, or DC shifts) and trigger stimulation to abort the seizure. For motor BCI: decoded movement intention triggers stimulation of motor cortex or spinal cord.

Design the control law. Simplest: threshold-based on/off control (if beta power exceeds threshold, stimulate at fixed parameters; below threshold, stop). This works for responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy (NeuroPace RNS). For smoother control in Parkinson's: proportional control where stimulation amplitude scales linearly with beta power above a baseline. More advanced: model-predictive control using a transfer function model from stimulation input to biomarker output (identified from open-loop data), optimizing stimulation trajectory to track a desired biomarker setpoint.

Analyze closed-loop stability. The neural system introduces delays: stimulation takes 0.5-2 seconds to affect beta power in Parkinson's. If the controller gain is too high relative to the loop delay, oscillations occur (stimulation cycles on and off at a frequency related to the delay). Use control theory: model the plant (brain response to stimulation as a first-order system with delay), design the controller with adequate phase margin (greater than 45 degrees). Set a maximum stimulation amplitude hard limit that cannot be exceeded by the control law under any biomarker input.

Define safety bounds and fallback. Maximum stimulation amplitude must never exceed the charge density safety limit regardless of biomarker input. Rate-limit parameter changes (no more than 10% amplitude change per second) to prevent abrupt transitions. If the biomarker signal is lost (electrode failure, artifact contamination), fall back to open-loop stimulation at the last known effective parameters. Log all biomarker values and parameter adjustments for clinician review. Include a patient-controlled emergency stop.

description: Fabricate a microelectrode array from wafer-level micromachining through metallization, packaging, and quality control for implantable neural recording.

steps.description: Fabricate the electrode array substrate using silicon micromachining or polymer thin-film processing, defining the shank geometry and dielectric layers.

inputs.name: electrode-design
inputs.desc: Array geometry (shank count, length, width, pitch), substrate material (silicon, polyimide, parylene-C), and target impedance

outputs.name: fabricated-substrate
outputs.desc: Patterned substrate wafer with shank geometry, dielectric layers, and alignment marks for subsequent metallization

outputs.name: substrate-process-record
outputs.desc: Process parameters for each fabrication step (etch depth, deposition thickness, lithography alignment) and in-process QC measurements

process: For silicon-based arrays (Utah array style): start with a 500 um thick silicon wafer. Define electrode columns by dicing a grid of 400 um deep cuts on the backside, leaving an array of protruding columns on the front. Etch columns to needle shape using wet isotropic etch (HNA: HF/nitric/acetic) or DRIE (Bosch process for straight sidewalls followed by isotropic SF6 for tip sharpening). Target: 50-80 um diameter shank, 1-1.5 mm length, tip radius under 5 um for low-trauma insertion.

For polymer-based arrays (Michigan style on polyimide): spin-coat polyimide (HD Microsystems PI-2611, 10-20 um per layer) on a silicon carrier wafer with a sacrificial release layer. Cure at 350 degrees C under nitrogen. Pattern the shank outline using oxygen plasma RIE through an aluminum hard mask. For parylene-C substrates: deposit 5-10 um parylene by CVD (Gorham process) at room temperature, pattern by O2 plasma with photoresist mask.

Deposit the dielectric insulation layer. For silicon substrates: thermally grow 500 nm SiO2 followed by 200 nm LPCVD Si3N4 (dual-layer for pinhole reduction). For polymer substrates: the polymer itself serves as the dielectric; add a 1 um parylene-C barrier layer if using polyimide (parylene has lower moisture permeability). Verify dielectric integrity by measuring leakage current at 5 V DC in saline: must be below 1 nA per electrode site.

Perform in-process metrology: measure shank dimensions (optical microscopy, SEM for tip geometry), dielectric thickness (profilometry, ellipsometry), and surface roughness (AFM if electrode sites require sub-nm roughness characterization). Record all process parameters (etch rate, deposition rate, chamber conditions) for traceability.

steps.description: Deposit and pattern the electrode metal traces and recording sites to achieve the target impedance and charge injection capacity.

inputs.name: fabricated-substrate
inputs.desc: Patterned substrate with dielectric layers

inputs.name: electrode-design
inputs.desc: Recording site diameter, material choice, and impedance target

outputs.name: metallized-array
outputs.desc: Electrode array with patterned metal traces and exposed recording sites

outputs.name: impedance-map
outputs.desc: Measured impedance at 1 kHz for every electrode site across the wafer, with yield and uniformity statistics

process: Deposit the conductor metal stack by sputtering or e-beam evaporation. Standard stack: 20 nm titanium adhesion layer, 200-500 nm gold or platinum conductor, 20 nm titanium cap. For traces that must be thin and flexible: 200 nm gold on 20 nm Cr adhesion layer. Platinum is preferred for electrode sites due to superior electrochemical stability; gold is acceptable for traces that will be insulated.

Pattern metal using lift-off or wet/dry etch. Lift-off: spin photoresist, lithographically pattern, deposit metal, dissolve resist to lift off unwanted metal. Works well for features above 5 um. For sub-micron features, use dry etch (Ar ion milling of Pt, Cl2-based RIE for Au/Ti) with a hard mask. Alignment accuracy between metal layer and shank geometry must be within 2 um.

Open recording sites by etching the top dielectric in defined windows. Site diameter determines impedance: 15 um diameter bare Pt site gives 500 kOhm to 1 MOhm at 1 kHz. To reduce impedance, electroplate with high-surface-area coatings: platinum black (electrodeposited from chloroplatinic acid, reduces impedance to 10-50 kOhm), iridium oxide (AIROF by pulsed electrodeposition, also gives high charge injection capacity for stimulation, 1-4 mC/cm2), or PEDOT:PSS (electropolymerized from EDOT monomer in PSS solution, impedance 5-30 kOhm). Each coating has different long-term stability.

Measure impedance at 1 kHz for all sites using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy in PBS at room temperature. Apply a 10 mV RMS sinusoidal excitation. Calculate yield: percentage of sites within 2x of median impedance. Typical yield target: greater than 90%. Sites with impedance greater than 5x median indicate fabrication defects (incomplete metallization, residual dielectric). Reject or rework defective sites.

steps.description: Package the fabricated electrode array into a functional implantable assembly including connector, cable, and hermetic enclosure for the electronics.

inputs.name: metallized-array
inputs.desc: Electrode array with patterned traces and verified recording sites

inputs.name: encapsulation-design
inputs.desc: Encapsulation material and feedthrough design

outputs.name: packaged-assembly
outputs.desc: Complete electrode array assembly with connector or wireless module, ready for sterilization

outputs.name: assembly-test-results
outputs.desc: Electrical continuity, impedance verification, insulation resistance, and mechanical integrity test results

process: Release the electrode array from the carrier wafer. For silicon arrays: singulate by dicing or laser cutting. For polymer arrays on sacrificial release layers: dissolve the release layer (aluminum in KOH, copper in ammonium persulfate) and carefully peel the flexible array from the carrier. Handle with care: polymer arrays are fragile during release.

Bond the array to its cable or flex circuit. Wire bonding (wedge bonding with 25 um gold or aluminum wire) connects array bond pads to a flexible printed circuit (FPC). For high-channel-count arrays, use flip-chip bonding with anisotropic conductive film (ACF) or gold stud bump bonding for hundreds of connections in a small area. Each bond adds series resistance (typically 0.1-1 Ohm per bond, negligible compared to electrode impedance).

Assemble into the housing. Attach the FPC cable to the hermetic housing feedthrough using connector or direct solder. Encapsulate the cable and transitions with medical-grade silicone (NuSil MED-4211) for flexibility and biocompatibility. For wireless assemblies: mount the ASIC, antenna coil, and battery/capacitor inside the titanium housing. Route the electrode lead out through the hermetic feedthrough. Pot internal connections with epoxy to prevent vibration damage.

Test the completed assembly. Electrical continuity: verify every channel from electrode tip to external connector/wireless output. Insulation resistance: apply 5 VDC between each channel and ground (saline bath), verify greater than 1 MOhm per channel. Impedance: re-measure all sites in PBS to confirm no degradation from assembly (impedance should be within 20% of pre-assembly values). Mechanical: pull-test the cable-to-housing junction to 2 N minimum without failure. Leak test the hermetic housing with helium leak detection (below 10^-8 atm-cc/s).

description: Design, train, and validate a brain-computer interface decoder from feature selection through model architecture, closed-loop adaptation, and session-to-session transfer.

steps.description: Select and extract neural features that carry the most information about the intended variable, matched to the signal type and BCI application.

inputs.name: sorted-spike-trains
inputs.desc: Single-unit and multi-unit spike trains from neural recording

inputs.name: lfp-features
inputs.desc: LFP band power features

inputs.name: behavioral-data
inputs.desc: Ground truth behavioral measurements (hand position/velocity, speech audio, cursor target position) time-aligned to neural data

outputs.name: feature-matrix
outputs.desc: Neural features extracted at each time bin (channels x features x time), with feature labels and bin size

outputs.name: feature-information-analysis
outputs.desc: Mutual information or R-squared between each feature and the behavioral target, guiding feature selection

process: Define the time bin size from the application latency requirement. For continuous cursor control: 50-100 ms bins provide a good trade-off between temporal resolution and firing rate estimation reliability (a neuron firing at 20 Hz gives 1-2 spikes per 50 ms bin, Poisson-limited). For speech BCI: 20-50 ms bins to capture fast articulatory dynamics. For discrete selection: trial-averaged features over 200-500 ms windows.

Extract features by signal type. From spike trains: firing rate (spike count / bin duration), or threshold crossings per bin if spike sorting is not used (multi-unit activity, which is more stable across days). From LFP/ECoG: band power in relevant bands (high gamma 70-200 Hz from ECoG is the most informative for motor and speech decoding, extracted as the analytic amplitude of the bandpass-filtered signal). From EEG: mu rhythm (8-12 Hz) and beta (13-30 Hz) desynchronization over motor cortex.

Perform feature selection. Calculate the mutual information or correlation (R-squared) between each neural feature and the behavioral target at multiple time lags (neural activity leads behavior by 50-200 ms in motor cortex). Select the top N features that provide the highest decoding performance in cross-validation, using forward selection or L1 regularization. For high-dimensional feature spaces (1000+ channels x multiple features), PCA or factor analysis first reduces dimensionality to 20-100 latent factors, then decode from factors.

Handle non-stationarity. Neural feature distributions shift across minutes (adaptation), hours (electrode drift), and days (chronic changes). Z-score features within each session block (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation of a recent calibration window). This normalization preserves relative modulation while removing baseline shifts. For features with log-normal distributions (firing rates), apply log transform before z-scoring.

steps.description: Select the decoder model architecture, train on calibration data, and optimize hyperparameters using nested cross-validation.

inputs.name: feature-matrix
inputs.desc: Neural features at each time bin

inputs.name: behavioral-data
inputs.desc: Ground truth targets

inputs.name: feature-information-analysis
inputs.desc: Feature relevance rankings

outputs.name: trained-decoder
outputs.desc: Decoder model with fitted parameters and hyperparameters

outputs.name: offline-performance-metrics
outputs.desc: Cross-validated R-squared, MSE, classification accuracy, and information transfer rate

process: Select architecture by application. For 2D cursor control from motor cortex spikes: Kalman filter (state = [x, y, vx, vy], observation = firing rates). Linear, interpretable, updates in closed-form, very low latency (under 1 ms to compute). For 3D arm kinematics: Kalman filter or unscented Kalman filter if nonlinearities are significant. For discrete classification (grasp types, phonemes): LDA if features are approximately Gaussian, or gradient-boosted trees for nonlinear boundaries. For high-dimensional temporal sequences (speech from ECoG): RNN (GRU or LSTM) or temporal convolutional network, trained end-to-end.

Train on calibration data. For Kalman filter: closed-form solution. State transition matrix A from regressing state at t+1 on state at t. Observation matrix C from regressing firing rates on state. Noise covariances W and Q from residuals. For neural networks: train with Adam optimizer, learning rate 1e-3 to 1e-4, batch size 32-128, for 50-200 epochs with early stopping on validation loss. Use dropout (0.2-0.5) for regularization with small datasets (common in neural data, often under 10 minutes of calibration).

Hyperparameter optimization. Use 5-fold cross-validation with temporal splits (not random, to respect time structure). For Kalman filter: optimize the bin size, number of neural features, and time lags included. For neural networks: optimize hidden layer size, dropout rate, learning rate, and number of layers. Use Bayesian optimization (Gaussian process) or random search over the hyperparameter space. Report the mean and standard error of the performance metric across folds.

Measure offline decoding performance. For continuous targets (velocity): Pearson correlation r (typically 0.7-0.9 for motor BCI with intracortical arrays), R-squared (variance explained), and mean squared error. For discrete targets: classification accuracy, confusion matrix, Cohen's kappa (chance-corrected accuracy). Calculate information transfer rate for comparison across studies. Typical: 2-4 bits/s for intracortical motor BCI (cursor control), 0.5-1 bit/s for ECoG speech BCI, 0.1-0.5 bits/s for EEG motor imagery BCI.

steps.description: Adapt the decoder during closed-loop BCI use to account for user learning and neural non-stationarity, using intention-aware recalibration.

inputs.name: trained-decoder
inputs.desc: Initial offline-trained decoder

inputs.name: offline-performance-metrics
inputs.desc: Baseline offline accuracy

outputs.name: adaptive-decoder
outputs.desc: Decoder with online adaptation algorithm enabled, including learning rate and update schedule

outputs.name: closed-loop-performance-metrics
outputs.desc: Online performance metrics (target acquisition time, path efficiency, success rate, throughput in bits/s) from closed-loop testing

process: Identify the online-offline performance gap. Decoders trained on offline calibration data (user performs movements, neural data is recorded) typically underperform when used online (user observes decoded cursor and adapts behavior). The gap arises because the user's neural strategy changes under closed-loop feedback. Expect 20-50% performance reduction initially, recovering as user and decoder co-adapt.

Implement ReFIT-style intention estimation. During closed-loop cursor control, the true user intention is not known (unlike offline calibration where target movement is measured). Estimate intention by assuming the user always intends to move the cursor toward the target. Re-label the training data: replace the actual cursor velocity (which includes decoder errors) with the vector pointing from current cursor position to target position. Retrain the Kalman filter observation model on this corrected data. This typically doubles the bit rate compared to non-adaptive decoding.

For continuous adaptation: use recursive least squares (RLS) or stochastic gradient descent to update decoder parameters every N minutes using the most recent data with intention-estimated labels. Set the learning rate to balance tracking non-stationarity (higher rate) against stability (lower rate). A forgetting factor of 0.99-0.999 per sample in RLS gives good results. Monitor decoder stability: if decoded output variance suddenly increases, freeze adaptation and revert to last stable parameters.

Measure closed-loop performance with standardized tasks. Center-out reaching (Fitts's law): cursor starts at center, 8 targets appear at equal angles, measure acquisition time and path efficiency (straight-line distance / actual path length). Calculate throughput in bits/s using Fitts's law: TP = ID / MT, where ID = log2(D/W + 1), D is target distance, W is target width, MT is movement time. State-of-art intracortical BCI: 2-3 bits/s throughput, comparable to an assistive eye-tracker. Compare to offline predictions and quantify the online-offline gap closure from adaptation.

steps.description: Design the decoder recalibration strategy for stable day-to-day BCI use without full recalibration, using transfer learning and alignment techniques.

inputs.name: adaptive-decoder
inputs.desc: Decoder with adaptation capability

inputs.name: closed-loop-performance-metrics
inputs.desc: Within-session performance

outputs.name: transfer-learning-strategy
outputs.desc: Method for cross-session decoder initialization (zero-shot, few-shot, alignment-based) with expected warm-up time and accuracy

outputs.name: long-term-stability-assessment
outputs.desc: Performance trajectory over weeks and months, identifying degradation sources and their mitigations

process: Characterize day-to-day neural instability. Between sessions (next day), neural recordings change: single-unit tuning properties shift (preferred direction rotates, gain changes), some units disappear and new ones appear (electrode micromotion), baseline firing rates drift. These changes mean a decoder trained on day 1 data performs poorly on day 2 without recalibration (typically 50-80% accuracy drop for Kalman filter on raw spike features).

Implement alignment-based transfer. LFADS (Latent Factor Analysis via Dynamical Systems) or MINT (Modular Inverse Neural Transform) extract low-dimensional neural dynamics that are more stable than individual neuron tuning. Train the decoder on the latent factors rather than raw firing rates. Day-to-day alignment: find a linear mapping (Procrustes alignment) between day N latent space and the original training day latent space. This typically recovers 70-90% of within-session accuracy without any calibration data on the new day.

For few-shot recalibration: collect 2-5 minutes of calibration data on the new day (user performs a short target acquisition task). Use this data to update the observation model (Kalman filter C matrix) or fine-tune the last layer of a neural network decoder. This typically recovers 90-100% of within-session accuracy. The trade-off is calibration time: users prefer zero calibration, but 2 minutes of calibration dramatically improves the rest of the session.

Assess long-term stability. Track daily performance metrics (throughput, success rate, calibration time needed) over months. Identify trends: does performance gradually decline (electrode degradation, increasing glial scar) or remain stable with recalibration? For chronic arrays (Utah), typical trajectory: stable performance for 6-12 months with daily recalibration, then gradual decline as unit yield drops. Strategies to extend functional life: use multi-unit threshold crossings instead of sorted single units (more stable across months), use LFP features (stable for years but lower information content per channel), or transition to a combination of spike and LFP features as single units are lost.

description: Design a rigorous electrophysiology experiment from protocol development through statistical power analysis, data management, and ethical compliance.

steps.description: Design the behavioral task, trial structure, and recording protocol to answer the scientific question with adequate statistical power.

inputs.name: research-question
inputs.desc: The specific hypothesis to test or the neural phenomenon to characterize

inputs.name: recording-capabilities
inputs.desc: Available recording system (electrode type, channel count, signal type, recording duration limits)

outputs.name: experimental-protocol
outputs.desc: Detailed task design (stimuli, timing, conditions, trial count), recording parameters, and session structure

outputs.name: power-analysis
outputs.desc: Required sample size (trials per condition, sessions, subjects) to detect the expected effect size with specified power

process: Define the experimental conditions from the hypothesis. For a motor encoding study: conditions might be reach directions (8 directions, center-out). For a cognitive study: conditions might be task difficulty levels or stimulus categories. Ensure conditions are balanced and counterbalanced to avoid order effects. Include catch trials or null conditions to estimate baseline activity and false-positive rates.

Design the trial structure with precise timing. Define epochs: fixation (500-1000 ms), cue/stimulus (variable by design), delay (if testing working memory, 0.5-3 s), response (movement, speech, button press), inter-trial interval (1-3 s, jittered to prevent anticipatory responses). Total trial duration determines how many trials fit in a session. For intracortical recording in behaving primates: 1-2 hour sessions are typical, giving 300-600 trials for a simple center-out task (3-4 seconds per trial including ITI).

Calculate statistical power. For spike rate comparisons between conditions: effect size is the difference in firing rate divided by the standard deviation across trials. With typical neural variability (Fano factor approximately 1), detecting a 20% rate modulation (e.g., 20 Hz vs 24 Hz, SD approximately 5 Hz) gives Cohen's d approximately 0.8. At alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8, need approximately 25 trials per condition per neuron (paired comparison). For population-level decoding: the minimum training set size depends on feature dimensionality. As a rule of thumb: 10 trials per class per feature dimension for LDA, more for nonlinear classifiers.

Plan recording sessions. If testing N conditions with M trials each at T seconds per trial: session duration = N x M x T / 3600 hours. Add 20% overhead for rest periods, reward delivery, and equipment checks. For chronic recording studies, plan the recording schedule across days/weeks to capture both within-session and across-session variability. Document the complete protocol in sufficient detail for replication.

steps.description: Execute a recording session with proper equipment setup, quality checks, and real-time monitoring to maximize data quality.

inputs.name: experimental-protocol
inputs.desc: Task design, timing, and recording parameters

outputs.name: session-data
outputs.desc: Recorded neural data with behavioral timestamps, quality annotations, and metadata

outputs.name: session-quality-report
outputs.desc: Channel impedances, noise levels, unit yield, behavioral performance, and any anomalies during the session

process: Pre-session equipment check. Measure electrode impedances at 1 kHz using the recording system's built-in impedance test. Flag channels with impedance greater than 2 MOhm (possible broken electrode) or less than 10 kOhm (possible short to reference or ground). Check the noise floor: with inputs connected to the headstage but subject at rest, RMS noise should be below 5 uV in the spike band and below 10 uV broadband. Check reference and ground connections: poor reference shows as correlated 60 Hz noise across all channels.

Configure the recording system. Set the sampling rate (30 kSps for spike recording, 1 kSps for LFP-only). Set the gain to use the full ADC range without clipping: for a +/- 500 uV input range on 16-bit ADC, the LSB is 15 nV, adequate. Enable hardware filters: 0.3-6000 Hz bandpass for spike channels, 0.1-300 Hz for LFP. Set up event synchronization: connect behavioral task system to the recording system via digital event lines (TTL pulses marking trial start, stimulus onset, response, reward).

Monitor data quality during recording. Display a rolling spectrogram or RMS plot to detect artifacts in real time. Watch for: sudden impedance changes (electrode movement), sustained 60 Hz increase (ground or reference issue), broadband noise bursts (motion artifact, cable connector issue). If quality degrades, pause and troubleshoot before continuing. Track behavioral performance: task completion rate should exceed 80% to ensure adequate trial counts.

Post-session data management. Save raw data in a standardized format: Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) for archival, or the recording system's native format plus conversion scripts. Record metadata: date, subject ID, electrode map, channel impedances, experimental conditions, task parameters, session notes. Back up data immediately to a second location. Log the session in a lab notebook or database with quality annotations (good session, partial data loss on channels X-Y, behavioral engagement level).

steps.description: Analyze electrophysiology data with appropriate statistical methods, multiple comparison corrections, and reproducibility measures.

inputs.name: session-data
inputs.desc: Recorded neural data with behavioral timestamps

inputs.name: research-question
inputs.desc: Hypothesis to test

outputs.name: analysis-results
outputs.desc: Statistical test results, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and population-level summaries

outputs.name: analysis-code-package
outputs.desc: Complete, executable analysis pipeline (preprocessing, feature extraction, statistical tests, figure generation) for reproducibility

process: Preprocess: artifact removal (see neural-artifact-removal chain), spike sorting (see spike-detection-and-sorting chain), LFP feature extraction (see lfp-spectral-analysis chain). Align neural data to behavioral events using the digital event timestamps. Define analysis windows relative to events (e.g., 200 ms before movement onset to 500 ms after).

Single neuron analysis. For each neuron, test whether firing rate differs between conditions using ANOVA (if comparing 3+ conditions) or t-test (2 conditions), with trial as the unit of observation. Report effect size (eta-squared for ANOVA, Cohen's d for t-test) alongside p-values. Apply multiple comparison correction across neurons: Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction at q = 0.05, which is less conservative than Bonferroni and more appropriate for neural populations where many neurons are expected to be modulated.

Population-level analysis. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on population firing rate vectors to identify dominant patterns of activity. Neural state-space analysis: project population activity into the top 2-3 PCs and plot trajectories for different conditions. Decoding analysis: train a classifier (LDA, SVM) on population activity to determine how much condition information is present, using leave-one-out or stratified k-fold cross-validation. Report classification accuracy with 95% confidence interval from bootstrap.

Ensure reproducibility. Write the complete analysis pipeline as executable code (Python with NumPy/SciPy/scikit-learn, or MATLAB). Pin software versions. Use random seeds for reproducibility. Include the raw data path, all preprocessing parameters, statistical test specifications, and figure generation code. Data and code should be organized for sharing (e.g., DANDI archive for NWB data, GitHub for analysis code). Pre-register the analysis plan before data collection if testing a specific hypothesis (not exploratory).

description: Navigate the regulatory pathway for a neural device from FDA classification through biocompatibility testing, clinical trial design, and submission.

steps.description: Classify the neural device under FDA regulations and identify the appropriate premarket pathway (510(k), De Novo, or PMA).

inputs.name: device-description
inputs.desc: What the device does, its intended use, how it contacts the body (implanted, external, duration), and its risk level

inputs.name: predicate-device-search
inputs.desc: Results of searching FDA databases (510(k), PMA, De Novo) for similar devices already cleared or approved

outputs.name: regulatory-classification
outputs.desc: FDA product code, classification (Class I, II, or III), and recommended premarket pathway with rationale

outputs.name: regulatory-strategy
outputs.desc: Timeline, key submissions, standards to meet, and estimated cost for the selected pathway

process: Determine device classification. Most neural recording devices are Class II (510(k)) if they have a predicate (e.g., EEG systems with predicate to existing cleared EEG devices, product code GWQ). Implantable neural stimulators are typically Class III (PMA) due to high risk: deep brain stimulators (product code PFG), responsive neurostimulators (NeuroPace RNS is the predicate for seizure-responsive stimulation). Novel BCI devices with no predicate may use the De Novo pathway to establish a new classification.

For 510(k): identify a legally marketed predicate device with the same intended use and similar technological characteristics. If the new device differs from the predicate in technology (e.g., wireless vs wired), prepare to demonstrate substantial equivalence through bench testing, biocompatibility, and possibly clinical data. Performance data must show the new device is at least as safe and effective as the predicate. Timeline: 3-6 months for FDA review after submission.

For PMA (Class III): this requires clinical evidence of safety and effectiveness. Plan for an IDE (Investigational Device Exemption) to conduct a clinical trial before submission. The PMA submission includes: device description, manufacturing information, bench testing, biocompatibility (ISO 10993), electrical safety (IEC 60601), software documentation (IEC 62304), EMC testing, sterility validation, clinical trial data, and labeling. Timeline: 1-3 years for clinical trial plus 6-12 months for FDA review. Cost: typically 1-5 million USD for the clinical trial plus regulatory consultants.

For all pathways: identify applicable consensus standards. IEC 60601-1 (general safety and essential performance), IEC 60601-1-2 (EMC), IEC 62304 (software lifecycle for medical devices), ISO 14708 (implantable medical devices), ISO 10993 (biocompatibility), ISO 11607 (packaging validation), ISO 11135 or 11137 (sterilization). FDA recognizes these standards: declaring conformity reduces review burden. For cybersecurity of connected neural devices: follow FDA guidance on premarket cybersecurity (threat modeling, SBOM, update mechanism).

steps.description: Design the clinical trial for a neural device including endpoints, patient population, trial structure, and safety monitoring.

inputs.name: regulatory-classification
inputs.desc: FDA pathway and classification

inputs.name: device-description
inputs.desc: Device function, intended use, target patient population

outputs.name: clinical-trial-protocol
outputs.desc: Trial design (randomized, single-arm, crossover), sample size, primary and secondary endpoints, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and duration

outputs.name: ide-submission-outline
outputs.desc: Structure of the IDE application including preclinical data package, risk analysis, and informed consent elements

process: Define the primary endpoint from the intended use. For a BCI typing device: typing speed in characters per minute compared to baseline (no-device) condition. For a DBS device for Parkinson's: change in UPDRS motor score (Part III) from pre-implant baseline to 6 or 12 months post-implant. For a seizure-responsive stimulator: percent reduction in seizure frequency compared to a pre-implant baseline period. The primary endpoint must be clinically meaningful, objectively measurable, and previously used in neural device trials for comparability.

Determine sample size from the expected effect size and variability. For DBS in Parkinson's: existing data shows a mean UPDRS improvement of 10-15 points with SD of 8-10 points. To detect a 10-point improvement (Cohen's d approximately 1.0) at alpha = 0.05, power = 0.9, need approximately 20 subjects per group. For a single-arm trial (no control group, comparing to baseline): approximately 15 subjects. Add 20% for dropout. For first-in-human BCI studies: initial safety cohorts may be as small as 3-5 subjects under a feasibility IDE.

Design the trial structure. For high-risk neural devices: a staggered enrollment is typical (first 3 subjects implanted sequentially with a safety review between each, then enrollment opens). Include a blinded assessment period if possible (for stimulation devices: randomize to stimulation ON vs OFF periods, with the patient blinded). Follow-up: minimum 1 year for implantable devices, with scheduled assessments at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. Record all adverse events (device-related and procedure-related) with severity and relatedness classification.

Prepare the IDE submission package. Sections: (1) device description and intended use, (2) prior investigations (bench testing, animal studies with chronic implant histology, biocompatibility testing per ISO 10993), (3) risk analysis (ISO 14971, with risk/benefit for each identified hazard), (4) manufacturing summary (design controls per 21 CFR 820), (5) clinical investigation plan (the protocol above), (6) informed consent document (must include: surgical risks, device risks, alternative treatments, right to withdraw, long-term follow-up obligations), (7) IRB approval. Submit to FDA: 30-day default review, FDA may place a clinical hold if deficiencies are identified.

steps.description: Design the post-market surveillance system for a neural device to monitor long-term safety, track device performance, and comply with reporting requirements.

inputs.name: clinical-trial-protocol
inputs.desc: Clinical endpoints and safety monitoring plan

inputs.name: device-description
inputs.desc: Device characteristics and risk profile

outputs.name: post-market-plan
outputs.desc: Complaint handling, MDR reporting procedures, post-market clinical follow-up study design, and corrective action triggers

outputs.name: cybersecurity-post-market-plan
outputs.desc: Vulnerability monitoring, patch management, coordinated disclosure process for connected neural devices
