process: Establish complaint handling per 21 CFR 820.198. Every patient or clinician complaint must be logged, investigated, and classified (device malfunction, adverse event, use error). For neural implants: track electrode impedance trends from follow-up visits (progressive increase may indicate encapsulation failure), stimulation threshold changes (may indicate lead migration), and infection rates (typically 2-5% for cranial implants).

Define Medical Device Reporting (MDR) triggers per 21 CFR 803. Report to FDA within 30 days: any death or serious injury where the device may have caused or contributed, and any malfunction that would likely cause or contribute to death or serious injury if it recurred. For neural devices, reportable events include: lead fracture, infection requiring explant, hemorrhage from implant procedure, unexpected stimulation effects, device malfunction requiring surgical intervention. Track complaint trends to detect emerging signals.

Design post-market clinical follow-up (PMCF). For PMA devices: FDA may require a post-approval study as a condition of approval. Typical: enroll 100-500 additional subjects at multiple sites, follow for 3-5 years. Track the same primary endpoint as the pivotal trial plus long-term safety (5-year infection rate, lead integrity, battery longevity). For devices marketed in the EU under MDR: PMCF is mandatory, with periodic safety update reports (PSUR) submitted to the notified body annually.

For connected/wireless neural devices: implement a cybersecurity post-market plan. Monitor for vulnerabilities in the device software, wireless communication protocol, and connected systems (clinician programmer, patient controller). Establish a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process. Design and validate a secure firmware update mechanism for the implanted device (if applicable) or external components. Test updates on bench before deployment. Maintain a software bill of materials (SBOM) and monitor for CVEs in third-party components.

description: Design a wireless telemetry system for an implantable neural device covering data link, power transfer, antenna, and SAR compliance.

steps.description: Calculate the wireless data link budget for transmitting neural data through tissue, selecting the modulation scheme and data rate from the channel count and compression strategy.

inputs.name: telemetry-design
inputs.desc: Required data rate after compression, link range through tissue, BER target

inputs.name: implant-constraints
inputs.desc: Available power for transmitter, antenna size constraint, SAR limit

outputs.name: link-budget-analysis
outputs.desc: Transmit power, path loss through tissue, receiver sensitivity, link margin, and achievable data rate

outputs.name: modulation-coding-selection
outputs.desc: Selected modulation (OOK, FSK, BPSK, QPSK), coding (convolutional, LDPC), and protocol

process: Estimate path loss through tissue. For inductive near-field (13.56 MHz) at 1-2 cm separation through skin and skull: coupling loss is dominated by coil geometry and alignment, typically 20-30 dB. For far-field UWB (3-10 GHz) through 1 cm tissue: path loss = free-space path loss + tissue attenuation. Tissue attenuation at 4 GHz: approximately 3-4 dB/cm for skin, 5-7 dB/cm for bone, 1-2 dB/cm for brain. Total one-way loss through 1 cm skin + 0.5 cm bone: approximately 7-10 dB above free-space.

Calculate link budget: Received power (dBm) = Transmit power (dBm) + TX antenna gain (dBi) - Path loss (dB) + RX antenna gain (dBi). For an implant transmitting at -10 dBm (0.1 mW, well within SAR limits) with a small patch antenna (-15 dBi implant, 0 dBi external), and 40 dB total path loss at 4 GHz: received power = -10 + (-15) - 40 + 0 = -65 dBm. Receiver sensitivity for 10 Mbps BPSK at BER 10^-6: approximately -80 dBm with a low-noise front end. Link margin = -65 - (-80) = 15 dB. Adequate for reliable operation with fading margin.

Select modulation scheme from power and data rate constraints. For low-power implants (below 1 mW TX): OOK (on-off keying) is simplest but spectral inefficient. FSK: slightly more complex, better noise immunity. BPSK/QPSK: best spectral efficiency but requires coherent receiver. For high data rates (above 10 Mbps), use OFDM over a UWB channel for multipath resilience. Add forward error correction: convolutional code (rate 1/2, constraint length 7) adds 3 dB coding gain. LDPC codes add 5-6 dB but require more decoding power.

Verify SAR compliance. Calculate the power deposited in tissue: SAR = sigma x |E|^2 / (2 x rho), where sigma is tissue conductivity, E is the electric field, rho is tissue density. For a small antenna radiating 0.1 mW in tissue with sigma = 0.5 S/m, rho = 1000 kg/m3: the peak SAR must be below 1.6 W/kg averaged over 1 g (FCC) or 2 W/kg over 10 g (ICNIRP). Run an EM simulation (FDTD or FEM) with a realistic head phantom model to verify. At 0.1 mW transmit, SAR is typically well below limits, but antenna near-field can create hotspots.

steps.description: Design the wireless power transfer system to charge or continuously power the implant through tissue using inductive, resonant, or ultrasonic coupling.

inputs.name: implant-constraints
inputs.desc: Total power requirement, implant depth, coil size constraint, duty cycle

inputs.name: power-delivery-design
inputs.desc: Whether battery-backed (intermittent charging) or continuous power required

outputs.name: wpt-design
outputs.desc: External and implant coil geometry, operating frequency, coupling coefficient, power transfer efficiency, and thermal profile

outputs.name: power-management-circuit
outputs.desc: Rectifier, regulator, and battery charging circuit design for the implanted receiver

process: Select WPT technology. Inductive coupling (100 kHz - 13.56 MHz): mature technology, used in cochlear implants, reliable at 1-2 cm through tissue, power up to several watts. Resonant coupling (6.78 MHz ISM band): higher efficiency at larger gaps and misalignment by exploiting coupled resonant modes, but more complex tuning. Ultrasonic power transfer: uses piezoelectric transducers at 1-5 MHz, smaller receiver size (millimeter-scale), but lower efficiency and complex acoustic path through bone. For most cranial neural implants: inductive at 13.56 MHz is the default.

Design the coil pair. External (transmit) coil: planar spiral, 30-50 mm diameter, 5-10 turns, Q factor 50-100. Implant (receive) coil: smaller, constrained by implant housing, typically 10-25 mm diameter, 10-20 turns, Q factor 20-50 (lower due to smaller size and proximity to lossy tissue). Calculate coupling coefficient k from coil geometry and separation: k = M / sqrt(L1 x L2), where M is the mutual inductance. For aligned coils at 1 cm separation with diameter ratio 2:1, k is approximately 0.1-0.2. Power transfer efficiency at optimal load: eta = (k^2 x Q1 x Q2) / (1 + k^2 x Q1 x Q2)^2 for series-parallel topology. At k=0.15, Q1=80, Q2=40: eta approximately 60%.

Design the implanted power management circuit. Rectifier: full-bridge rectifier using Schottky diodes (low forward voltage for efficiency) or active rectification with MOSFETs (for higher efficiency at higher power). Regulator: LDO for low-noise supply to analog circuits, buck converter for digital load. For battery-backed systems: add a lithium battery charging circuit (CC/CV charging, 4.2 V termination for LiCoO2, 3.6 V for LiFePO4). Battery capacity sizing: if the implant draws 20 mW continuous and charges for 30 minutes per day at 100 mW received power: daily energy budget = 20 mW x 24 h = 480 mWh. Charging delivers 100 mW x 0.5 h x 0.7 (charging efficiency) = 35 mWh. This does not balance: either charge more frequently, increase charging power, or reduce implant power consumption.

Verify thermal safety. The combined heat from coil losses (I^2R in the implant coil), rectifier losses, and electronics dissipation must not raise tissue temperature by more than 1 degree C (2 degree C absolute maximum). Run a thermal model: P_dissipated = P_received x (1 - system_efficiency). For 100 mW received at 60% coil efficiency and 80% electronics efficiency: dissipated = 100 x (1 - 0.6 x 0.8) = 52 mW. Spread over the implant surface area (e.g., 5 cm2): power density = 10.4 mW/cm2. This is below the commonly cited 40 mW/cm2 limit but should be verified by thermal simulation or measurement in a tissue phantom.

steps.description: Design the implant antenna for operation inside the body, accounting for tissue loading, size constraints, and coupling to the external system.

inputs.name: link-budget-analysis
inputs.desc: Operating frequency, required gain, bandwidth

inputs.name: implant-constraints
inputs.desc: Available volume for antenna, implant housing material (titanium, ceramic, polymer)

outputs.name: antenna-design
outputs.desc: Antenna type, dimensions, feed structure, simulated radiation pattern in tissue, and impedance matching

outputs.name: antenna-tissue-interaction
outputs.desc: Effect of tissue loading on resonant frequency, efficiency, and SAR distribution

process: Select antenna type from size and frequency constraints. For data telemetry at 2.4 GHz (Bluetooth/BLE) or 3-10 GHz (UWB): a planar inverted-F antenna (PIFA) or patch antenna fits inside a flat implant housing (10-25 mm diameter, 2-5 mm thick). For power transfer at 13.56 MHz: a planar spiral coil integrated into the implant housing or wound on a ferrite core. For combined data + power: dual-band or dual-antenna design with a 13.56 MHz coil for power and a UHF/UWB antenna for data.

Account for tissue loading. Human tissue has high relative permittivity (brain: epsilon_r approximately 50 at 2.4 GHz, muscle: approximately 53) and conductivity (brain: sigma approximately 1.8 S/m at 2.4 GHz). This drastically changes antenna behavior compared to free space: resonant frequency shifts down by roughly sqrt(epsilon_eff) (can be 30-50% lower), bandwidth broadens due to loss, and radiation efficiency drops to 1-10% because tissue absorbs most radiated power. Design the antenna dimensions for the in-body resonant frequency, not free-space.

Simulate the antenna in a realistic tissue model. Use a finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) or finite element (FEM) solver with a layered tissue model (skin 2 mm, fat 2 mm, bone 5 mm, brain) with frequency-dependent tissue properties from the Gabriel database. Place the antenna at the implant depth. Optimize dimensions (patch length, feed position) for impedance match (S11 below -10 dB at center frequency) and maximum radiation efficiency. Calculate the gain in the direction of the external receiver (typically broadside, through the skull). Expect realized gain of -20 to -30 dBi for a small implant antenna in tissue.

Optimize impedance matching between the antenna and the transceiver IC. The antenna impedance in tissue is complex and shifts with tissue composition and implant depth. Design a matching network (L-section or pi-network) with a tunable element (varactor or switched capacitor bank) to compensate for patient-to-patient variation. Alternatively, use a wideband antenna design that maintains adequate match (S11 below -6 dB) across the expected impedance variation range.

description: Design a closed-loop neuromodulation system from biomarker selection through detection algorithm, control law, and stability analysis for adaptive therapy.

steps.description: Identify and validate the neural biomarker that reliably tracks the disease state or symptom to serve as the control signal for adaptive stimulation.

inputs.name: therapeutic-objective
inputs.desc: Disease or symptom to modulate (Parkinson's tremor/bradykinesia, essential tremor, epileptic seizures, chronic pain, depression)

inputs.name: recording-capabilities
inputs.desc: Available neural signals (LFP from implanted leads, ECoG, scalp EEG, peripheral nerve)

outputs.name: validated-biomarker
outputs.desc: Selected biomarker (signal type, frequency band, spatial location), its correlation with symptom severity, and detection reliability metrics (sensitivity, specificity, latency)

outputs.name: biomarker-characterization-data
outputs.desc: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for biomarker-based symptom detection, showing the sensitivity-specificity trade-off at different thresholds

process: Survey candidate biomarkers from clinical literature. Parkinson's disease: beta (13-30 Hz) power in STN LFP correlates with bradykinesia and rigidity (r = 0.5-0.7 with UPDRS III). Gamma (60-90 Hz) activity increases with dyskinesia. Tremor has a specific tremor-frequency oscillation (4-6 Hz) in STN. Essential tremor: cerebellar-thalamic oscillation at tremor frequency. Epilepsy: pre-ictal changes (increased high-frequency oscillations 80-500 Hz, decreased low-frequency power) precede seizure onset by seconds to minutes. Chronic pain: theta (4-8 Hz) power in anterior cingulate cortex. Depression: theta/alpha ratio in prefrontal cortex (less established, still under research).

Collect paired biomarker-symptom data. Record the candidate neural signals continuously while simultaneously measuring symptom severity. For Parkinson's: record STN LFP during structured motor tasks (finger tapping, gait) with video-based UPDRS scoring by a blinded rater. For epilepsy: long-term monitoring (days to weeks) with simultaneous EEG/ECoG and seizure diary. For each time segment, extract the biomarker value (e.g., beta band power) and the corresponding symptom score.

Validate biomarker performance. Build a ROC curve: at each threshold of the biomarker, calculate sensitivity (true positive rate: correctly identifies high-symptom periods) and specificity (true negative rate: correctly identifies low-symptom periods). The area under the ROC curve (AUC) quantifies overall discriminability: AUC greater than 0.8 is good, greater than 0.9 is excellent. For Parkinson's beta power vs clinical state (ON/OFF medication): typical AUC is 0.8-0.9. For epileptic seizure detection: sensitivity greater than 90% is required clinically, with specificity determining false alarm rate.

Characterize biomarker dynamics. Measure the time course: how quickly does the biomarker change after stimulation onset? For Parkinson's beta: suppression begins within 0.5-2 seconds of stimulation onset, recovers within 1-5 seconds after offset. This time constant sets the minimum control loop update rate and influences controller design. Measure biomarker variability: within-session (minutes), across-session (days), across-patient. High inter-patient variability means the threshold must be individualized.

steps.description: Design the real-time biomarker detection algorithm for embedded implementation on the implanted processor, meeting latency and power constraints.

inputs.name: validated-biomarker
inputs.desc: Selected biomarker with detection parameters

inputs.name: implant-constraints
inputs.desc: Available processing power (embedded microcontroller or ASIC), memory, power budget for signal processing

outputs.name: detection-algorithm
outputs.desc: Algorithm specification (filtering, feature extraction, classification), detection latency, computational cost, and real-time performance metrics

outputs.name: embedded-implementation-specification
outputs.desc: Fixed-point arithmetic precision, memory footprint, MIPS requirement, and power consumption estimate

process: Design the feature extraction pipeline for embedded execution. For beta band power detection: bandpass filter (13-30 Hz, 4th-order IIR Butterworth, computationally inexpensive), then rectify (absolute value), then low-pass smooth (2 Hz cutoff, single-pole IIR). This produces a running estimate of beta power with approximately 250 ms latency from the smoothing filter. Total computation: approximately 10 multiply-accumulates per sample at 500 Hz sampling rate, trivial for any microcontroller.

For seizure detection (more complex): extract multiple features from the LFP in sliding windows (2-second windows, 50% overlap). Features: power in multiple frequency bands (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma, high-gamma), line length (sum of absolute sample-to-sample differences), and coastline (similar but amplitude-normalized). Classify using a linear discriminant or small neural network (2 hidden layers, 16 units each). Total computation: approximately 1000 operations per classification, feasible for a low-power ARM Cortex-M4 at under 1 mW.

Implement in fixed-point arithmetic for embedded deployment. Convert all floating-point operations to Q15 or Q31 fixed-point format. Use CMSIS-DSP library functions for IIR filters and matrix operations on ARM processors. Verify that fixed-point numerical error does not degrade detection performance: compare classification accuracy between floating-point and fixed-point implementations on the same test dataset. Acceptable degradation: less than 2% accuracy loss.

Validate real-time performance. Run the algorithm on the target processor with real neural data streamed at the actual sample rate. Measure: worst-case execution time per processing cycle (must be less than the inter-sample interval), memory usage (must fit in available SRAM), and power consumption (measure total processor current draw during operation). Detection latency from biomarker change to algorithm output: target less than 500 ms for Parkinson's, less than 2 seconds for seizure onset detection (to allow time for stimulation to abort the seizure).

steps.description: Design the control law that maps biomarker values to stimulation parameter adjustments, including stability analysis and safety bounds.

inputs.name: detection-algorithm
inputs.desc: Real-time biomarker output specification

inputs.name: stimulation-parameters
inputs.desc: Adjustable parameter range (amplitude, frequency, pulse width)

inputs.name: biomarker-characterization-data
inputs.desc: Biomarker-symptom correlation and stimulation response dynamics

outputs.name: control-law-specification
outputs.desc: Control algorithm (threshold, proportional, PID, model-predictive), parameter mapping function, update rate, and safety constraints

outputs.name: stability-and-safety-analysis
outputs.desc: Closed-loop stability verification (phase margin, gain margin), safety bound analysis, and failure mode response

process: Model the plant (brain response to stimulation). From open-loop data (step changes in stimulation amplitude while recording biomarker): identify a transfer function. For Parkinson's beta power response to STN stimulation: approximately a first-order system with gain K (beta suppression per mA of stimulation, typically 20-40%/mA) and time constant tau (0.5-2 seconds for beta onset, 1-5 seconds for offset). Include a pure time delay of 200-500 ms for neural processing. Plant model: G(s) = K x exp(-delay x s) / (1 + tau x s).

Design the controller. For proportional control: stimulation amplitude = K_p x (biomarker - setpoint), where setpoint is the desired biomarker level (e.g., 50th percentile of beta power distribution). Choose K_p for adequate response without oscillation: the gain margin should be at least 6 dB and phase margin at least 45 degrees. For the first-order plant with delay above: the maximum proportional gain before instability is approximately tau / (K x delay). With tau = 1 s, K = 0.3/mA, delay = 0.3 s: max K_p approximately 11 mA. Use K_p = 3-5 mA for adequate margin.

Add safety constraints. Hard limits: minimum stimulation amplitude = 0 (no negative stimulation), maximum amplitude = the maximum safe value from charge density analysis. Rate limits: no more than 0.5 mA change per second to prevent abrupt transitions that could cause transient side effects. If the biomarker signal quality drops (amplitude below noise floor, or artifact detected): freeze stimulation at current level for a timeout period (10-30 seconds), then ramp to a safe open-loop default. All transitions must be smooth (ramp, not step) to avoid patient discomfort.

Simulate the closed-loop system. Use the plant model and controller to simulate the response to: (1) step change in symptom state (e.g., medication wearing off, increasing beta), (2) biomarker noise (random fluctuations), (3) sensor dropout (biomarker signal lost for 5 seconds). Verify: no oscillations in stimulation amplitude, settling time within acceptable clinical range (under 30 seconds for Parkinson's), no overshoot beyond safety limits. Validate the simulation against actual closed-loop recordings from clinical studies if available (Adaptive DBS trials show 30-50% energy savings vs continuous stimulation with equivalent symptom control).
